papers.title: Agentic AI in Automated Markets
papers.abstract: Automated markets increasingly host autonomous, learning trading agents and are powered by formulaic automated market makers (AMMs). We study how heterogeneous agent behavior shapes stress, risk-adjusted performance, liquidity, and volatility in these types of markets. Three behavioral archetypes are modeled as agentic reinforcement learning (RL) systems: a rational arbitrageur, a manipulator, and a retail herd-follower. Each archetype is defined by its reward function within a common, asset-agnostic exposure-control environment, and each is trained with a value-based Deep Q-Network (DQN) and with REINFORCE using a learned baseline. A pilot on hourly cryptocurrency data (AAVE, ETC, SUI) motivates the hypotheses. Herd-followers produce the most frequent but shortest stress episodes, manipulators the fewest but most persistent, and rational agents the most stable rolling Sharpe ratios despite higher return volatility. SHAP attributions tie these patterns to drawdown and cross-asset signals, short-term volatility and position state, and momentum, respectively. The results motivate behavior-specific regulation rather than uniform limits on volatility or turnover.

papers.title: Cointegrated Regressors: Where Folded Concave Penalties Go Beyond LASSO
papers.abstract: LASSO is one of the most popular regularization methods for high-dimensional regression models. While cointegration is common in practical applications of predictive regressions with many regressors, the convex penalty of LASSO overly suppresses the coefficients of cointegrated regressors and therefore fails to deliver consistent parameter estimation. We employ folded concave penalties (FCP), including the well-known SCAD and MCP, to address this issue. Using FCP, we establish two asymptotic results: (i) a local oracle property for the penalized regression, and (ii) a global oracle property for regressions with a penalty-level constraint. In particular, the latter guarantees a global solution that consistently estimates the true coefficients and enjoys oracle prediction performance. Simulation studies and an application to predicting the euro area unemployment rate show that FCP improves variable selection and out-of-sample prediction relative to LASSO.

papers.title: Online Conditional Vine Copulas: Forecasting Electricity Demand
papers.abstract: We propose an online multivariate distributional forecasting model in which we condition the parameters of a vine copula on covariates. An online algorithm updates the parameters sequentially using only the most recent observations. Existing approaches require full batch re-estimation using all available data at each update step, which makes them computationally slow in large-scale forecasting applications and less suitable for settings in which dependence structures change over time. Simulation results show that the online procedure achieves forecasting performance comparable to that of the batch estimator, while reducing computation time substantially. We illustrate the method in a forecasting application to electricity net-demand across five regions of Great Britain and show that (i) the conditional vine copula model outperforms unconditional Gaussian and vine copula benchmarks and (ii) that online estimation improves forecast accuracy when batch re-estimation is not available. The algorithm is implemented in the Python package ondil.

papers.title: SLIM: Stochastic Learning and Inference in Nonlinear GMM Models
papers.abstract: We propose SLIM (Stochastic Learning and Inference in overidentified Models), a new scalable stochastic approximation algorithm for nonlinear GMMs with many nonseparable moments and parameters. SLIM is shown to be consistent and asymptotically normal without a consistent initial estimator or a globally convex GMM criterion. Random-scaling and plug-in based confidence set constructions remain valid when computational uncertainty can be non-negligible relative to sampling uncertainty. An optional second-order refinement achieves full-sample GMM efficiency. We develop $J$-tests for SLIM. The theoretical results are extended to models with clustered data of unequal cluster sizes. Monte Carlo experiments for a nonlinear demand system with 576 moments and 380 parameters demonstrate computational gains and scalability to one million observations. A LinkedIn application with 4.8 million college graduates illustrates clustered estimation and inference for first employment destinations.

papers.title: Estimation of Panel Data Models with Nonlinear Factor Structure
papers.abstract: Panel data models with unobserved heterogeneity in the form of interactive effects standardly assume that the time effects -- or ``common factors'' -- enter linearly. This assumption is restrictive because it concerns an unobserved component of the model, for which a particular functional form is rarely justified. By contrast, linearity in the observable regressors can often be motivated by economic theory or empirical convention. Linearity in the factors has persisted mainly because it is convenient and improves on standard fixed effects. This paper relaxes that assumption by combining the common correlated effects (CCE) approach with sieve methods. The resulting estimator -- abbreviated ``SCCE'' -- preserves key advantages of CCE, including computational simplicity and good small-sample and asymptotic properties, while allowing for a broader class of factor structures that nests the linear case. This makes it suitable for a wide range of empirical applications.

papers.title: (Debiased) Inference for Fixed Effects Estimators with Three-Dimensional Panel and Network Data
papers.abstract: Inference for fixed effects estimators is often unreliable due to Nickell- and incidental parameter biases. While these issues are well understood for classical two-dimensional panels, little is known about three-dimensional panel structures (e.g., sender x receiver x time). We develop inferential theory for a broad class of linear and nonlinear fixed effects M-estimators in this setting, covering bipartite, directed, and undirected network panel data, multiple specifications of additively separable unobserved effects, and both strictly exogenous and predetermined regressors. Our analysis reveals fundamentally different asymptotic properties compared to two-dimensional panels. In particular, we find a sharp dichotomy across specifications: (i) when unobserved effects vary along a single panel dimension, estimators are asymptotically unbiased, (ii) when they vary along two panel dimensions, estimators may suffer from a severe inference problem characterized by a degenerate asymptotic distribution. We resolve the latter by deriving explicit bias formulas and proposing analytically debiased estimators with nondegenerate, correctly centered asymptotic distributions. An empirical application studies dynamic network formation in a directed panel of bilateral trade relationships.

papers.title: Causal Identification under Interference: The Role of Treatment Assignment Independence
papers.abstract: Applied researchers often use identification formulas derived under individualistic treatment response (ITR), which rules out interference, even when interference is plausible but unobserved. We characterize what these identification formulas recover under arbitrary interference. For selection on observables, instrumental variables, sharp regression discontinuity, and difference-in-differences, each ITR-based formula equals an average direct effect (ADE)-type estimand plus a bias. Every term of the bias is the product of an interference component and a component measuring how the law of others' assignments differs across the two comparison groups. The bias therefore vanishes under a restriction on the assignment mechanism, generalized conditional assignment independence (CAI), whose design-specific forms include conditions used in the literature. Because generalized CAI cannot generally be tested from the single realization of the assignment vector observed in data, we develop a sensitivity analysis that relaxes it and derive identified sets, together with the corresponding breakdown frontiers and breakdown points, under arbitrary interference. When interference is anonymous and operates through a treated share, the structure yields tighter bounds indexed by a measure of assignment dependence that can be benchmarked with observed group-level assignment patterns. A calibrated simulation and a reanalysis of a temporary-agency employment study illustrate the paper's theoretical results and proposed sensitivity-analysis procedures.

papers.title: Inference for Fixed Effects Estimators when Panels are Unbalanced
papers.abstract: We develop the asymptotic theory for two-way fixed effects M-estimators in unbalanced panels, within a framework where both panel dimensions grow large at proportional rates. The selection process may be deterministic, stochastic, or a combination of the two. We require neither a missing-at-random condition nor a selection equation, only a conditional mean restriction on the outcome. The uncorrected estimators are asymptotically normal but not correctly centered due to incidental parameter bias and feedback bias. The latter arises when regressors or the selection indicator respond to past outcomes. We propose debiased estimators that remove both biases without requiring knowledge of which regressors or selection components are predetermined. Simulations show that the corrections remove most of the bias and restore coverage close to nominal levels. Revisiting a study on capital inflow surges and banking crises, we find that the corrections leave qualitative conclusions unchanged but substantially shift the estimated magnitudes.
